d: The classic group of infections that cross the placenta or reach the newborn at birth: Toxoplasma, other agents (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, Zika), rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex.
Abnormal fluid in two or more fetal compartments, such as skin edema, ascites and pleural or pericardial effusion; parvovirus B19 causes it through severe fetal anemia and high-output heart failure.
Intravenous penicillin G, or ampicillin, given during labor to a group B strep carrier at least 4 hours before birth; it prevents early-onset neonatal GBS disease but not late-onset disease.
The late signature of congenital syphilis: notched, peg-shaped upper incisors called Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis of the cornea and eighth-nerve (sensorineural) deafness.
A test of how tightly IgG binds its antigen; low-avidity IgG means a primary infection within the past few months, while high-avidity IgG means the infection is older.

The change of a patient's antibody test from negative to positive, shown by IgG turning positive between two samples. In pregnancy it proves a new, primary infection, the situation with the highest risk to the fetus.
